# 2 Clement — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Author** | Anonymous (NOT Clement of Rome — the attribution is a later error) |
| **Date** | c. 140–160 CE |
| **Audience** | A Greek-speaking Christian community, possibly Corinth or Rome |
| **Genre** | Homily (sermon) — the earliest complete Christian sermon to survive |
| **Timeline** | Mid-second century, during the first major phase of Christian theological synthesis |
| **In One Sentence** | The oldest surviving Christian sermon — anonymous, earnest, and theologically rich — calling a congregation to repentance, ethical seriousness, and recognition of the pre-existent female Church as their true mother. |

---

## The World Behind the Text

Second Clement is not by Clement, is not a letter, and has almost nothing to do with 1 Clement. It was grouped with 1 Clement in the manuscript tradition (it follows 1 Clement in Codex Alexandrinus and in the Syriac manuscript tradition) and therefore inherited the name, but the attribution was recognized as spurious at least by the sixteenth century. What we have is a homily — that is, a sermon delivered to an assembled congregation, probably to be read aloud at a worship gathering, most likely by a figure of some authority in the community.

The world the sermon addresses is one of settled Christian community life in the mid-second century. The congregation knows its scriptures (largely the Septuagint); it has heard the Gospels read aloud (the sermon quotes or alludes to what appears to be the Gospel of Matthew and possibly the Gospel of Luke, and perhaps a non-canonical gospel as well); and it is in need, apparently, of a serious call to repentance. The preacher's concern is not heresy or schism but spiritual complacency — the danger that people who have received the grace of conversion and baptism will fail to live up to what that grace demands.

The community addressed appears to be predominantly Gentile. There is no engagement with Torah observance, no concern with Jewish-Christian boundaries, and the preacher writes as though the break with Judaism is long settled. The theology is essentially "proto-orthodox" — not Gnostic, not Marcionite, not obviously aligned with any of the major mid-second-century heterodox movements — but it is a theology still in the process of formation, with some ideas that feel genuinely archaic and others that feel remarkably developed.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

The sermon's explicit purpose is to call the congregation to repentance and moral earnestness. Chapter after chapter, the preacher insists that baptism is not a free pass, that salvation is not guaranteed by the mere fact of having converted, and that what God requires is a life of sustained ethical transformation: "Let us repent with our whole heart, that none of us may perish by the way." The repetition is not tedium — it is pastoral urgency. The preacher is worried about people who have settled into a comfortable religion of nominal membership without ethical consequence.

But the sermon has a second, more theologically striking purpose: to articulate a doctrine of the Church as a pre-existent spiritual reality, specifically as feminine — as the Bride of Christ and indeed as the mother of believers. Chapter 14 contains one of the most remarkable passages in all of early Christian literature: "The books and the apostles declare that the Church was not founded now, but was from the beginning. For she was spiritual, as was also our Jesus; but he was manifested in the last days that he might save us. And the Church, being spiritual, was manifested in the flesh of Christ, showing us that if anyone of us keep her in the flesh and do not corrupt her, he shall receive her in the Holy Spirit."

The Church is pre-existent. The Church is female. The Church is identified with the Spirit. This is not Gnostic language — the preacher is not using "spiritual" to mean "non-material in a disparaging sense." It is a high theology of the church's reality that has largely been forgotten in later tradition, though traces of it appear in Paul (Galatians 4:26, "the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother") and in the Shepherd of Hermas.

---

## How to Read This Book

Second Clement is short — 20 chapters — and can be read in 30 minutes. But it should be read as what it is: a sermon. That means it was designed to be heard, not read privately. Its rhythms are oral. Its arguments circle back on themselves in the way that good preaching does. Its emotional register shifts from urgency to tenderness to warning to encouragement.

Read chapter 1 with care: "Brethren, we ought to think of Jesus Christ as of God, as of the Judge of living and dead." This is the opening sentence, and it sets the doctrinal register immediately — a high Christology in which Christ is not merely a teacher or prophet but the divine judge of all humanity. The entire sermon proceeds from this premise.

Read chapter 14 as the theological center. The concept of the pre-existent female Church is the most distinctive and historically significant idea in the text. The preacher is not inventing this — he seems to be drawing on a tradition — but he develops it with remarkable confidence. After reading it, go back to Paul's Galatians 4 and Ephesians 5 and you will read those passages differently.

Read chapters 15–19 as the sermon's conclusion, in which the preacher argues that the reward of the faithful is not escape from the body but resurrection of the flesh. This is significant: the preacher is explicitly arguing against a spiritualized, disembodied salvation, and doing so in a world where Gnostic Christianity was offering exactly such a spiritualized alternative. The insistence on bodily resurrection in chapter 9 is blunt: "And let none of you say that this flesh is not judged and does not rise again."

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

The sermon's call to repentance connects it directly to the Shepherd of Hermas, the great second-century text devoted entirely to the possibility and method of post-baptismal repentance. Both texts address the same pastoral problem: what happens to Christians who sin after baptism? Is there a second chance? Both insist there is, emphatically, but both also insist the window may not remain open indefinitely.

The quotation in chapter 8 — "the Lord said: Even if you are gathered together with me in my bosom and do not do my commandments, I will cast you out and say to you, Depart from me; I do not know you, whence you are, you workers of lawlessness" — appears nowhere in the canonical Gospels. It may be from the Gospel of the Nazarenes, the Gospel of the Hebrews, or another lost early collection of Jesus sayings. This connects 2 Clement to the world of non-canonical gospel traditions documented also in the Gospel of Thomas.

The pre-existent female Church of chapter 14 connects to the Odes of Solomon, to Paul's "Jerusalem above" (Galatians 4:26), to the figure of Wisdom (Sophia) in Proverbs 8 and the Wisdom of Solomon, and to later developed Sophiology in Eastern Christian theology. It also connects, in a transformed way, to the Valentinian Gnostic concept of Sophia as a fallen feminine divine principle — both traditions are drawing on the same deep well of feminine divine symbolism.

The sermon's Gospel citations connect it to the complex world of second-century Gospel transmission, where Matthew, Luke, and non-canonical collections all circulated and were cited with equal authority.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

The most important thing to understand is that the congregation the preacher addresses has been baptized. The sermon is not evangelism — it is addressed to Christians. And the preacher's anxiety is not about intellectual doubt but about moral failure. The "repentance" being called for is not conversion from paganism but the ongoing conversion of a heart that has grown cold or complacent after its initial warming.

The concept of "flesh" in the sermon is more complex than it initially appears. When the preacher says "let us keep the flesh pure," he does not mean primarily sexual purity (though that is included). He means keeping the flesh — the embodied life — aligned with the Spirit, not indulging in the values and behaviors of the pagan world that surrounds the community. The "flesh" is the site of moral choice, and the preacher wants it to be the site of visible Christian witness.

The preacher's statement in chapter 13 that "the Gentiles, when they hear from our mouths the oracles of God, marvel at them for their beauty and greatness; then, when they find out that our deeds are not worthy of the words we speak, they turn from marveling to blasphemy, saying that it is some fable and delusion" is a remarkable piece of missional self-criticism: Christianity's credibility in the wider world depends entirely on the visible ethical quality of Christian lives. The sermon is in this sense profoundly evangelistic — though it addresses insiders, not outsiders.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

Second Clement's exclusion from the canon is almost entirely a matter of timing and attribution. By the time canonical decisions were being systematically made in the late fourth century, the text's pseudonymity was well enough understood that it lacked the apostolic credentials required for canonical standing. A sermon by an anonymous mid-second-century preacher — however orthodox, however edifying — could not compete with texts attributed (however debatably) to apostles.

The text survived because it was attached to 1 Clement in manuscript tradition, and 1 Clement survived because it was semi-canonical. Without that accidental attachment, 2 Clement might well have been lost entirely. The Codex Alexandrinus (fifth century) contains both 1 and 2 Clement appended after the New Testament. A Syriac manuscript tradition also preserves both texts.

The text is not included in the canon of any major Christian tradition today, though it is treasured as a patristic document. Eastern Orthodox and Catholic scholars regard it as an important early witness to mid-second-century Christian theology. Protestant historians value it for its window into early preaching practice and ecclesiology. Its greatest legacy may be its concept of the pre-existent female Church, which continues to surface in serious theological discussions about ecclesiology and divine femininity.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| c. 96–98 CE | 1 Clement written (the text 2 Clement will be attached to) |
| c. 140–160 CE | 2 Clement composed and delivered as a sermon |
| c. 200 CE | Clement of Alexandria cites similar ideas; both texts circulating |
| c. 313 CE | Eusebius mentions 1 Clement; 2 Clement less clearly distinguished |
| c. 400 CE | Both texts appear in Codex Alexandrinus after Revelation |
| c. 1056 CE | Bryennios's manuscript contains both (incomplete for 2 Clement) |
| 1875 CE | Bryennios publishes complete 2 Clement from Syriac manuscript |
| 1900s–present | Recognized as earliest complete Christian sermon |

---

*— HESED, Reader's Guide Division*
